content: Consequently, only a limited number of laboratories perform chlamydial cultures. In live birds, depending on the clinical signs they exhibit, combined choanal and cloacal swab specimens should be collected, refrigerated, and transported to the laboratory packed in ice, but they must not be frozen. Proper handling of these samples is critical to maintain the viability of the organisms for culture, and a specialized transport medium is required. It is recommended to contact the diagnostic laboratory for specific procedures regarding the collection and submission of specimens. Live birds being screened for Chlamydia psittaci may not shed the microorganism daily. To reduce laboratory costs, serial specimens should be collected over 3–5 consecutive days and pooled before culturing. Tissue samples from the bird's liver and spleen are the preferred necropsy specimens for isolating C. psittaci. Culture methods are recommended to avoid the limitations associated with other diagnostic tests. A positive serologic test result indicates that the bird was infected with C. psittaci at some point, but it does not necessarily confirm an active infection. False-negative results can occur in birds with acute infections if they are sampled before seroconversion. Additionally, treatment with antimicrobial agents can suppress the antibody response. A single testing method may not be sufficient due to the variability in immunoglobulin reactions across different avian species. Therefore, a combination of antibodyand antigen-detection methods is recommended, especially when testing a single bird. When specimens are obtained from a single bird, serologic testing is most useful when clinical signs of disease and the flock or aviary history are considered, and when serologic results are compared with white blood cell counts and liver enzyme activities. A greater than fourfold increase in titer from paired samples, or a combination of a titer and antigen identification, is required to confirm a diagnosis of avian chlamydiosis (AC). The advantages and disadvantages of specific serologic tests, such as direct complement fixation (CF) and elementary-body agglutination (EBA), are described below. Direct CF is more sensitive than agglutination methods, but false-negative results can occur in specimens from small psittacine birds (e.g., budgerigars, young African grey parrots, and lovebirds). High titers may persist after treatment, complicating the interpretation of subsequent tests. Modified direct CF is more sensitive than standard direct CF. EBA is commercially available and can detect early infections. Titers greater than 10 in budgerigars, cockatiels, and lovebirds, and titers greater than 20 in larger birds, are often observed in recent infections. However, elevated titers may persist even after treatment is completed. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) tests, such as QuickVue®, were initially developed for identifying Chlamydia trachomatis in humans but are now used to detect C. psittaci in birds. These tests provide rapid results and do not require live organisms, but false-positive results can occur due to cross-reacting antigens, and false-negative results may occur if insufficient antigen is present. As with all non-culture tests, ELISA results must be interpreted alongside clinical findings. If a bird has a positive ELISA result but appears clinically healthy, the veterinarian should attempt to confirm antigen shedding through organism isolation. Conversely, a negative ELISA result in a clinically ill bird does not rule out AC, and further testing (e.g., culture, serologic testing, or polymerase chain reaction [PCR]) is necessary. Immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) tests use monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies, fluorescein-staining techniques, and fluorescent microscopy to identify the organism in impression smears or other specimens. These tests share similar advantages and disadvantages with ELISA. PCR technology is offered by numerous laboratories for diagnostic testing. PCR is highly sensitive and specific for detecting target DNA sequences in collected specimens (e.g., choanal and cloacal swabs, blood). However, results from unvalidated tests can be challenging to interpret. Additional diagnostic techniques are either in use or under development. It is recommended to consult peer-reviewed reports on these methods before use. While current treatment protocols for avian chlamydiosis are generally effective, knowledge in this area is evolving, and no protocol guarantees safe treatment or complete eradication of the infection. Therefore, treatment for AC should be supervised by a licensed veterinarian. In quarantine situations, compliance may be easier to monitor when treatment is administered via medicated feed. All birds diagnosed with AC should undergo treatment for 45 days unless otherwise specified. Medicated feed should be the sole food provided during the entire treatment period. Birds' acceptance of medicated feed can vary, so food consumption should be monitored. Acceptance can be improved by first adapting the birds to a similar, non-medicated diet. Treatment begins once the birds accept the medicated feed as their sole diet. Options for medicated feed include: Medicated mash diets (e.g., >1% chlortetracycline with <0.7% calcium) prepared with corn, rice, and hen's scratch. Pellets and extruded products containing 1% chlortetracycline, which are suitable for most pet birds. The pellet size should be appropriate for the bird's size. Special diets may be necessary for lories and lorikeets, which naturally feed on nectar and fruit. Medicated water can also be used for treatment. Limited pharmacological studies suggest that dosages of 400 mg doxycycline hyclate per liter of water for cockatiels, and 400–600 mg per liter for African grey parrots, blue-fronted Amazon parrots, and Goffin's cockatoos, maintain therapeutic concentrations. Empirical use of 400 mg per liter has been successful for many psittacine birds (excluding budgerigars). However, drug toxicity can occur with this regimen, so an experienced avian veterinarian should monitor birds during treatment. Signs of toxicity include general illness (e.g., depression, inactivity, decreased appetite), green or yellow-stained urine, and altered hepatic test results (e.g., elevated aspartate aminotransferase, lactate dehydrogenase, and bile acids). If toxicity occurs, medication should be stopped immediately, and supportive care should be provided until the bird recovers. Treatment with a different regimen can be initiated later. Oral doxycycline is the drug of choice for treatment. Both the monohydrate and calcium-syrup formulations can be used. Recommended dosages are 40–50 mg/kg body weight orally once daily for cockatiels, Senegal parrots, and blue-fronted and orange-winged Amazon parrots, and 25 mg/kg body weight orally once daily for African grey parrots, Goffin's cockatoos, blue and gold macaws, and green-winged macaws. Precise dosages cannot be extrapolated for other species.
